overview: This file assembles U.S. diplomatic, consular, economic-intelligence, and interdepartmental reporting on Japan’s wartime shipbuilding and merchant-shipping crisis from 1941 through early 1944. Its principal item is Vice Consul Roy M. Melbourne’s comprehensive March 1943 report, based substantially on information and Japanese newspapers brought from Tokyo by Argentine attaché Ramon Lavalle, describing naval control of construction, government financing, material and labor shortages, production estimates, salvage, wooden ships, junks, rafts, and transport coordination. Reports from Bern add German-press information on Japanese and Manchurian construction programs, while captured-document translations and newspaper photographs illustrate wooden shipbuilding and salvage in Japanese-occupied territories. Correspondence from the Maritime Commission, Commerce Department, and State Department evaluates and commends the intelligence, which consistently identifies inadequate shipping as a critical Japanese vulnerability.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Japan’s shipbuilding industry
subfiles.about: A filing sheet points to a March 1941 letter attaching a report on conditions in Japan’s shipbuilding industry.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies the subject as the shipbuilding industry in Japan and notes that the referenced original attached a report on current conditions. It directs the reader to file 894.34/251 for the original paper.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Bern on financing Japanese merchant shipbuilding
subfiles.about: Harrison transmits a translated German newspaper account of Japanese government financing for merchant-ship construction.
subfiles.summary: A translated Frankfurter Zeitung article describes advances, bond issues, Industrial Bank credit, interest subsidies, and other state support intended to overcome the gap between controlled freight rates and rising construction costs. It says captured vessels supplied 220,000 gross tons and estimates that 500,000 gross tons of sunken shipping might be raised, of which nearly 50,000 tons had already been salvaged. Harrison highlights these estimates as evidence of Japan’s efforts to offset merchant-marine losses.

subfiles.title: Maritime Commission acknowledgment of Harrison’s report
subfiles.from: H. L. Vickery, United States Maritime Commission
subfiles.about: Vickery acknowledges receipt of Harrison’s report on the Japanese merchant-shipbuilding program.
subfiles.summary: The Maritime Commission confirms that it received the State Department’s July 18 memorandum enclosing Harrison’s June 17 despatch. Vickery states that the opportunity to study the translated German article is appreciated.

subfiles.title: Maritime Commission appreciation of Melbourne’s shipping report
subfiles.about: Deimel commends Vice Consul Melbourne’s report on Japanese wartime shipping and asks that such reporting continue.
subfiles.summary: Deimel states that he read Melbourne’s March 2 report with interest and appreciates the vice consul’s continuing efforts to obtain information. A routing annotation records that the report was referred to Saugstad for comment on March 30.

subfiles.title: Recommendation to grade Melbourne’s report “Excellent”
subfiles.about: The Far Eastern Affairs division recommends an “Excellent” grade for Melbourne’s attached shipping report.
subfiles.summary: The brief internal note recommends the highest stated evaluation for Melbourne’s study of Japanese wartime shipping. Its title mistakenly gives the terminal date as January 1942, although the attached report covers June 1942 through January 1943.

subfiles.title: Internal assessment of Melbourne’s sources and initiative
subfiles.about: An internal memorandum explains Melbourne’s use of Ramon Lavalle as a source and recommends that Melbourne be commended.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies the report as a continuation of Melbourne’s earlier survey covering December 1941 to June 1942. It explains that the new material became possible after former Argentine Embassy attaché Ramon Lavalle arrived in Istanbul from Tokyo. Officials are directed to the report’s summary and newspaper illustrations, and Melbourne’s initiative is praised.

subfiles.title: Japanese Wartime Shipping, June 1942 to January 1943
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Vice Consul; approved by Burton Y. Berry
subfiles.about: A comprehensive intelligence report assesses Japanese shipping, shipbuilding, labor, finance, salvage, and improvised transport during the war.
subfiles.summary: Drawing on Japanese press material collected by Ramon Lavalle and Melbourne’s experience at Kobe, the report portrays merchant shipping as a fundamental Japanese weakness and estimates total 1942 naval and commercial construction at about 800,000 tons. It describes naval control, state financing, high costs, shortages of steel, machinery, and skilled labor, and doubts about Japan’s ability to adopt mass-production methods. Separate sections examine salvage, wooden vessels, motorboats, sailboats, junks, ocean-going timber rafts, harbor development, transport coordination, insurance, and training. The report concludes that continued Allied destruction of Japanese shipping could damage industrial production and elite morale and suggests using motor torpedo boats against small coastal craft.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: “Towed From Hokkaido”
subfiles.from: Japanese press, enclosed by the American Consulate General at Istanbul
subfiles.about: A photograph and caption describe the trial voyage of a 60,000-cubic-foot timber raft from Hokkaido to Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: The caption claims that a tug successfully towed the ocean-going timber raft through storms and heavy seas. It presents the voyage as a means of augmenting Japan’s transport capacity and shows Premier Hideki Tojo inspecting the raft at Shibaura.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: “Aim: Self-Supply in Southern Regions”
subfiles.to: Enclosed with the Istanbul shipping report
subfiles.about: A photographic clipping depicts new construction and repair of small vessels in the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The caption says Japanese forces and local inhabitants were constructing shipping locally to meet transport needs. It identifies the newly launched vessel Akebono Maru, of more than 200 tons, and shows a formerly enemy-owned craft undergoing repairs for service among Philippine ports.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: “Navy Men Lead War”
subfiles.to: Enclosed with the Istanbul shipping report
subfiles.about: A photographic clipping shows Imperial Japanese Navy personnel refitting a vessel at Makassar.
subfiles.summary: The clipping presents ship repair and reconstruction in the occupied Southern Regions as an energetic naval undertaking. Its surviving caption identifies a reopened shipbuilding plant at Makassar; the remainder of the text is truncated after mentioning abandoned motorcars.

subfiles.title: Commerce Department praise for Melbourne’s report
subfiles.from: Charles K. Moser, forwarded by George Wythe
subfiles.about: The Commerce Department asks that Melbourne be thanked for exceptionally useful intelligence on Japanese shipping.
subfiles.summary: Moser calls the report the most comprehensive recent material available on Japanese shipping and valuable for assessing Japan’s current situation. Because reliable information from Japan and Japanese-controlled areas was scarce, he recommends encouraging consular officers to question people returning from the Far East.

subfiles.title: State Department commendation to Melbourne
subfiles.from: G. Howland Shaw, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Burton Y. Berry, American Consul, Istanbul
subfiles.about: The State Department informs Berry that Melbourne’s report was graded “Excellent” and asks him to convey official commendation.
subfiles.summary: The letter praises Melbourne’s initiative and confirms that his confidential despatch received an “excellent” grade. It quotes Henry L. Deimel’s appreciation on behalf of the Maritime Commission and asks Berry to bring the comments to Melbourne’s attention.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference for telegram no. 1554
subfiles.about: A filing notation records the transfer of telegram no. 1554 to another decimal-file classification.
subfiles.summary: The slip references file 894.642/44. It states that telegram no. 1554 was transferred to file 846B.642/8 but supplies no substantive text or date.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Bern on Japan’s 300-ton wooden ships
subfiles.about: Hamilton summarizes German reports about rapidly constructed Japanese wooden sailing ships intended to save strategic materials.
subfiles.summary: The German press reportedly described ship no. 101, a 300-ton wooden vessel built in 35 days with methods saving 20–35 percent of materials and eliminating the former wood-drying period. Although wooden ships formed only a small part of the program, they were said to be valuable for carrying goods from southern territories. The report illustrates their potential with claims about transporting sugar for Japan’s population and iron sufficient to build additional ships.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Bern on requisitioned motor sailing ships
subfiles.about: Harrison reports Japan’s expanded requisitioning and centralized allocation of motor sailing ships.
subfiles.summary: As a sequel to the October 16 telegram, Harrison states that Japan lowered the requisition threshold for motor sailing ships from 70 to 50 tons. Several thousand requisitioned vessels were placed under a central organization for allocation among fourteen shipping companies to maximize carrying capacity.

subfiles.title: Memorandum describing captured Japanese photostats
subfiles.about: An internal note identifies attached photostats as translations of captured Japanese material.
subfiles.summary: The first described sheet contains a photograph and account of a new Japanese 250-ton wooden ship. The second contains translations of Japanese military orders, linking shipbuilding intelligence with captured operational records.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s Liaison Office routing sheet
subfiles.from: Department of State, Under Secretary’s Liaison Office
subfiles.to: Listed State Department divisions and offices
subfiles.about: A routing form directs that the attached captured material circulate through designated offices and then return to the Liaison Office.
subfiles.summary: The sheet consists principally of a table of departmental routing abbreviations. It contains no substantive shipbuilding information but documents the internal circulation of the attached intelligence.

subfiles.title: Exhibit B: First 250-ton wooden ship launched at Osaka
subfiles.from: Allied Translator and Interpreter Section material
subfiles.about: A translated Japanese clipping reports the ceremonial launch of a standard 250-ton wooden vessel in Osaka.
subfiles.summary: The clipping says the vessel was the first and largest of five standardized wooden-ship types and had been constructed by carpenters working continuously since November. It records the attendance of shipbuilding and maritime officials, including Takata, Moriwaki, Nomi, and Takashima, and describes the freshly timbered hull entering an Osaka canal. The clipping itself was dated April 20, but its year was not given; the intelligence header records receipt in September 1943.

subfiles.title: ATIS Bulletin No. 495: Osaka wooden ship and captured military orders
subfiles.about: The bulletin combines another translation of the Osaka wooden-ship clipping with extracts from captured Japanese military orders from New Guinea.
subfiles.summary: The first item substantially duplicates the account of the first 250-ton standardized wooden ship launched in Osaka. The second summarizes Japanese dispatches and orders dated March–September 1943, including losses of landing craft to enemy torpedo boats, command changes, and evacuation of hospital patients by landing craft and fishing boats through Kirige, Karaiya, and Garobe to Rabaul. It also notes a captured sketch of Tsurubu aerodrome and its vicinity.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Bern on Manchurian shipbuilding at Dairen
subfiles.about: Harrison reports German claims about tankers and passenger-freighters under construction at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The report says new Manchurian government yards expected to complete two 8,000-gross-ton ocean-going tankers by mid-1944. Together with four smaller existing tankers, they were to form an independent Manchurian tanker fleet, while two 4,500-ton combined passenger-freight vessels were also under construction.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Bern on seven NYK motor freighters
subfiles.about: Harrison relays a German report that Nippon Yusen Kaisha ordered seven fast motor freighters from Mitsubishi at Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Each proposed freighter was reportedly to displace 9,300 tons and make 18 knots when fully laden. The German press claimed that Mitsubishi would complete all seven vessels during 1944.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Bern on Shimada’s shipbuilding claims
subfiles.about: Harrison reports Marine Minister Shimada’s parliamentary claim that Japanese shipbuilding output was rapidly doubling.
subfiles.summary: According to a Tokyo dispatch published in the German press, Shimada told Parliament that shipbuilding was progressing favorably. He claimed that 1943 production had doubled the 1942 figure and that 1944 output had a good prospect of doubling again.

interest: The file is especially valuable because it shows how U.S. officials reconstructed Japan’s maritime position from an unusual mixture of neutral-country diplomacy, German and Japanese press reports, an Argentine diplomat’s collected material, and captured Japanese documents. Melbourne’s report offers unusually broad coverage of the improvisations forced by shipping shortages—from salvage and standardized wooden hulls to junks, sailboats, and timber rafts—and explicitly connects maritime attrition with Japanese industrial capacity and elite morale. The commendation and routing papers also reveal how wartime economic intelligence was evaluated and circulated across State, Commerce, and the Maritime Commission. Historians should nevertheless distinguish measured observations from Japanese or German propaganda claims, especially the optimistic production forecasts and assertions about the performance of improvised vessels.
